blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Define revenue, and keep the income a firm takes in apart from the costs it pays out.

blocks.heading: Income from selling
blocks.text: Revenue is the income a firm receives from selling its output over a period, measured in money and before any costs are deducted. It is read in two ways: total revenue, the whole income from sales in the period, and average revenue, that income per unit sold. A lodge at the Etosha gate that fills 20 rooms at N$1 500 a night takes in N$1 500 x 20 = N$30 000 for those nights; that income is its revenue, whether or not it covers the lodge's costs. A bus operator in Windhoek, a tailor in Katutura and a coffee roaster in the Netherlands earn revenue the same way: money comes in from sales before wages, rent or materials are paid.

blocks.heading: Revenue is not profit
blocks.text: Revenue and profit are different measures, and mixing them up ruins any judgement about a firm. Revenue counts the money coming in from sales; profit is what remains after the costs of production are paid, so profit is total revenue minus total cost. A firm can take a large revenue and still make a loss, where its costs are larger still; a firm with modest sales can be profitable where its costs are small. The two are told apart by asking what is being counted: sales income alone, or sales income set against the payments the firm makes.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: The costs these earnings are set against come from sections 3.7.1 and 3.7.2; the calculations that turn price and sales into revenue figures are section 3.7.4, and the aims a firm pursues with what remains are section 3.7.5.
